claim_text: Claude Code offers seven methods for instructing behavior — CLAUDE.md files, rules, skills, subagents, hooks, output styles, and appending the system prompt — and each trades context cost against authority by controlling when an instruction loads, whether it survives compaction, and how much weight it carries
evidence_span: Each method trades context cost against authority.

claim_text: An instruction is the wrong tool for something that absolutely must not happen: under pressure, in a long session, in an ambiguous situation, or through a prompt injection in a file the task reads, the model can fail to follow a prompted rule, so a real guardrail has to be deterministic — hooks and permissions
evidence_span: Claude will follow the instruction most of the time, but when under pressure, in a long session or an ambiguous situation, or due to a prompt injection in a file accessed as part of the task, the model can fail to follow a prompted rule.

claim_text: In a shared repository CLAUDE.md grows the way any unowned config file does, and because every line loads into every session for every engineer whether relevant or not, it consumes tokens and dilutes adherence to the instructions that actually matter
evidence_span: This consumes tokens and dilutes adherence to the instructions that actually matter.

claim_text: Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, give it an owner, and review changes to it like code — pushing team-specific conventions into path-scoped rules and procedures into skills as it grows
evidence_span: Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, give it an owner, and review changes to it like code.

claim_text: An unscoped rule is mechanically identical to putting the content in CLAUDE.md — always loaded, always costing tokens — so a rule that applies to one part of the tree earns its keep only through a paths field that keeps it out of context during unrelated work
evidence_span: An unscoped rule is mechanically identical to putting the content in CLAUDE.md: always loaded, always costing tokens.

claim_text: A subagent's instructional body never enters the parent conversation at all: it runs in its own fresh context window and the only thing returning to the main session is its final message plus metadata
evidence_span: The subagent then runs in its own fresh context window, and the only thing that returns to your main session is the subagent's final message (often the aggregated result of many subtasks) plus metadata.

claim_text: Isolation is the main reason to reach for a subagent instead of a skill: a subagent suits a side task whose intermediate results would clutter the main conversation, while a skill suits a procedure you want to play out inside the main thread so you can see and steer each step
evidence_span: Use a skill when you want the procedure to play out inside the main thread so you can see and steer each step.

claim_text: A custom output style replaces rather than extends the default system prompt, dropping Claude Code's software-engineering instructions on scoping, comments, security, and verification unless keep-coding-instructions is set — which is why append-system-prompt, being purely additive, is the safer lever
evidence_span: By default, a custom output style drops all of this and Claude Code becomes more of a general assistant than a software engineer assistant.
